label: Recurrence
notes: Welcome to Lecture 5, spanning printed pages 27 through 32. We study why symplectic maps cannot lose volume, and how that single fact forces dynamical recurrence. The arc runs from the Liouville volume to Poincare's theorem and the area-preserving fixed-point results that open the door to symplectic rigidity.

label: The Liouville Volume
notes: Start by building the canonical volume from the symplectic form. The top power omega to the n, divided by n factorial, is a nowhere-vanishing form that orients the manifold. Because a symplectomorphism pulls back omega to itself, it pulls back every power, so it preserves this volume exactly.

label: Symplectomorphisms Preserve Volume
notes: Spell out the pullback computation so students see there is no slack. Preserving omega forces preservation of the wedge of n copies, hence of the Liouville form. This is the rigorous sense in which symplectic maps are volume-preserving, and it is the hinge for everything that follows in the lecture.

label: Hamiltonian Flows Are Volume-Preserving
notes: Apply the previous slide to time-t Hamiltonian flows, which are symplectomorphisms for every t. Their generator has zero divergence with respect to the Liouville volume, so phase-space volume is an exact invariant of the motion. Contrast this with dissipative flows that contract volume onto attractors.

label: Poincare Recurrence Theorem
notes: State the theorem carefully: a volume-preserving map of a finite-volume space returns almost every point arbitrarily close to its start, and does so infinitely often. Emphasize the measure-zero exceptional set and that no rate of return is promised, only its eventual certainty for almost every initial condition.

label: The Pigeonhole Proof
notes: Walk through the volume pigeonhole. Take a positive-volume neighborhood and iterate it. All images share the same volume, so inside a finite total volume they cannot stay pairwise disjoint forever. Two images must overlap, and pulling back gives a point of the set returning to the set.

label: Visual: Forced Overlap
notes: Read the diagram as a running area ledger. Each iterate of the neighborhood carries identical area, so the cumulative demand grows linearly without bound. Against a fixed finite ceiling that is impossible, forcing some pair of iterates to intersect. The intersection is the geometric heart of recurrence.

label: Consequences for Dynamics
notes: Draw the dynamical morals. Conservative Hamiltonian systems cannot possess universal attractors, since an attractor would shrink volume. Almost every orbit threads back near its origin endlessly. This also explains the apparent tension with thermodynamic irreversibility, resolved by astronomically long recurrence times.

label: Periodic Points and Fixed Points
notes: Shift from approximate return to exact return. Periodic points are fixed points of an iterate, and area-preserving surface maps are unexpectedly rich in them. This is where recurrence sharpens into the existence of genuine closed orbits, a theme that dominates the rest of the symplectomorphism story.

label: Poincare-Birkhoff Theorem
notes: Present the twist theorem flavor. An area-preserving homeomorphism of the annulus that rotates the two boundary circles in opposite senses must fix at least two interior points. Area preservation, not smoothness, supplies the count, which is why it foreshadows the rigidity phenomena of later lectures.

label: Toward Symplectic Rigidity
notes: Close by lifting the horizon. The forced fixed points of twist maps are the first hint that symplectic maps obey rigid existence laws far beyond mere volume preservation. This points directly at the Arnold conjecture and Gromov's nonsqueezing, the destinations the course is steering toward.
